column4: Support for the Local Governance Program
column5: Department of the Interior and Local Government
column6:
From 2017 to 2021, the SLGP served as a facility within the Department for improving local governance specifically in the areas of LDC Functionality, quality of Local Development Plans, horizontal and vertical integration of local plans, full-service delivery system, local asset management and resource mobilization.

As it gears up for its next five-year cycle from 2022 to 2027, SLGP 2.0 shall continue to address persisting local government issues that hamper local service delivery, and more decisively contribute to the vision of having empowered local governments providing excellent local service delivery through improved local development plans and institutionalized participatory governance mechanisms. The Program will also contribute towards the realization of Outcome 1 (Participatory Governance Deepened) and Outcome 2 (Public Accountability and Integrity Bolstered) of Chapter 14 (Practice Good Governance and Improve Bureaucratic Efficiency) of the PDP 2023 - 2028.

As a guide to achieve the desired outcomes of SLGP 2.0, all activities and initiatives of the Program will abide by three (3) key support pillars; namely: 1. Enhanced Overall Efficiency of Local Government Structures, 2. Strengthened Local Finances and Increased Fiscal Autonomy, and 3. Strengthened Good Governance at the Local Level.

column4: Public Management Development Program (PMDP)
Center of Excellence on Public Sector Productivity
column6:
Leading the movement on advancing innovation and productivity in the public sector across Asia and the Pacific region, the Philippines has been designated as the Asian Productivity Organization (APO) Center of Excellence on Public Sector Productivity with the DAP as the focal organization and implementing institution. The DAP also serves as the country’s National Productivity Organization (NPO) that supports the APO in promoting and implementing public sector productivity-related activities in the Asia-Pacific region.

As the implementing institution of the COE-PSP and the country’s NPO, the DAP is tasked to:
a. Facilitate learning and sharing of knowledge and best practices on PSP among APO members;
b. Conduct relevant research on new areas related to the PSP including identifying innovations and best practices;
c. Develop resources and materials to assist member countries with their programs; and
d. Engage experts and practitioners who could assist APO member countries with their programs on PSP.

The APO COE on Public Sector Productivity program has four key components: 
 a. PSP Knowledge Center
 b. PSP Capability Development Program 
 c. PSP Innovation Laboratory 
 d. PSP Research Program

column4: Government Quality Management Program (GQMP)
column6:
The Government Quality Management Program (GQMP) is a national government program that promotes and enhances quality improvement in the public sector. It was created through the issuance of Executive Order No. 605 s. 2007, Institutionalizing the Structure, Mechanisms, and Standards to Implement the Government Quality Management Program (GQMP).  The Program covers the provision of training and technical guidance to priority beneficiary agencies to develop their capabilities in establishing a Quality Management System (QMS), enhancing operational processes and controls, and developing the necessary documented information, among others. 

Specifically, the GQMP has the following components:
a. Government Quality Management Systems Standards (GQMSS) - Involves the development of a guidance document and the adaptation of relevant ISO management systems and standards that integrate relevant provisions of pertinent laws and/or rules and regulations to develop a culture of quality and integrity in governance characterized by citizen-focused and well-performing government organizations.
b. Advocacy and Capability Building (ACB) - Promote awareness, generate support, harness resources, and develop organizational capabilities in the establishment, implementation, and continuing improvement of quality management systems in public sector organizations.
c. Certification of Agencies’ QMS to GQMSS (PISO-QMS) - The Philippine Certification for ISO Quality Management Systems (PISO-QMS) shall be established to give due recognition to qualified government organizations that have demonstrated conformity of their QMS to the ISO 9001 and the GQMSS. As such, this component shall establish the structure and mechanisms to ensure the credibility of all aspects of certification in line with said standards.

column4: Program for Newly-Elected Officials (NEO)
column6:
The Local Government Academy (LGA) is fully committed to developing the capacities of local government officials to effectively perform, lead, and achieve their goals for better governance and improved service delivery through the Newly Elected Official Performing Leadership for Uplifting Service (NEO PLUS) Program where capacity development services is provided in a "three year duration" supporting these NEOs in their 3-year term of office.  In the last SGLG assessment 2024, only 41 out of 82 provinces, 96 out of 148 cities, and 577 out of 1,486 municipalities passed the assessment.  Also, local governments need to improve their absorptive capacities to transition and effectively manage programs that would be transferred to them due to the changes triggered by the Supreme Court ruling on the Mandanas-Garcia case.  While the Mandanas-Garcia ruling effectively improved LGU finances by creating a broader tax base for the National Tax Allotment, local finance data show that local governments continue to have limited capabilities of growing their local resources and depend on external sources of revenue.  Persistent challenges at the local government level continue, some of which are as follows:

● Boosting human capital to improve knowledge, skills and practices to support LGU good performance
● Improving client experience and satisfaction in the delivery of local government services 
● Modernizing processes and procedures and taking advantage of opportunities presented by new technologies
● Improving resilience in the face of broader geo-political tensions that affect local economies and environmental risks and challenges brought about by climate change and arising from human action
● Developing the local economy in the face of inflation, the incidence of poverty, and unmet basic needs
● Improving collaboration to converge and pool limited resources from various local governance stakeholders 

These challenges are the areas where the NEO PLUS Program will be addressing through series of training, coaching, mentoring, study visits and learning exchanges.  The NEO PLUS also contributes to the attainment of the Local Government Academy (LGA) Strategic Goal 1: Enhance the capacities of LGUs for effective local governance and local service delivery performance and its pressing mandate as articulated in Section 9 of Executive Order 138, the DILG through the LGA, is mandated to oversee capacity development interventions for local governments.  The LGA plays a crucial role in harmonizing all capacity development interventions provided by the National Government Agencies (NGAs) and other service providers to the LGUs.  In line with our role as harmonizer of Capacity Development initiatives, the implementation of the NEO PLUS program will be carried out in collaboration with several key partners.  These partners include DILG – Local Governance Regional Resource Centers (LGRRCs), DILG Sub-LGRCs, Local Government Leagues (such as the League of Provinces, League of Cities, League of Municipalities, and the Philippine Councilors League), NGAs who have expressed interest in being part of the program, and Local Research Institutes (LRIs).  This collaborative approach will be instrumental in ensuring the effective and efficient implementation of the NEO PLUS program and working together to achieve our shared goals.  Significantly, the NEO PLUS program is guided by the “Bagong Pilipinas” brand of governance of the President.

column4: Education and Training Capability Building Seminar
column6:
The Capability Building on Innovative Leadership for Legislative Staff (CBILLS) Program aims to strengthen the leadership, management, and technical skills of the members of the Philippine Congress, its officers, and staff through capacity-building interventions. It seeks to respond to the evolving training needs of the congressional machinery, enabling it to provide effective support in fulfilling its responsibilities for lawmaking and oversight.
With this agenda in mind, the CBILLS is designed and implemented as a continuous training development program that caters to the unique nature and operations of the Philippine Congress.
In line with the nation's development goals, all training interventions emphasizes the role of Congress in balancing government powers and adopting legislative measures addressing socio-political and economic issues.

The CBILLS aims to strengthen the legislative branch by providing capability building interventions that will enhance the required leadership and policy development competencies of legislative officers and staff according to three tracks, namely: Emerging Leaders, Middle Managers, and Senior Leaders. 

It is delivered through the following components, with specific objectives: 

Component 1: Local Training  which covers topics on management, leadership and technical skills, including special topics to revisit fundamental concepts, and facilitate awareness on current political trends, and new and/or emerging perspectives in the public sector.

Residential short courses on management, leadership and technical skills is a three to five-day training course designed specifically to enhance leadership competencies and technical skills of participants. It will involve lectures and practical application of concepts in the form of discussion, small group workshops and structured learning exercises. It enables participants to: 

Deepen their understanding of their management and leadership roles; 
Realize what it takes to be an effective leader/manager; 
Nurture their personal efficacy and ethical competence, and 
Hone their policy development competencies

Lecture series on socio-political and economic perspectives is an elective session of the CBILLS for the participants that aims to promote the discipline of long-term planning and to provide a venue for discussing strategic issues that impact socio-political and economic governance. It  enable participants to gain a wider perspective on socio-political and economic trends and innovations.

Component 2: International Learning Course (Observational Study Mission) which aims to expose participants to trends and best practices of model counterparts on legislative process, public policy system, public sector innovations and governance trends. It will also serve as a forum of information exchange where participants can discuss and share best practices, while building and strengthening network and collaboration with their counterparts.  It enables participants to develop a global mindset in realizing new strategies and best practices relevant to their work.

column4: Support to the Projects and Programs of the Productivity and Development Center (PDC)
column6:
The Philippines, as a founding member of the Asian Productivity Organization (APO), provides annual budgetary support to fulfill its commitments to regional cooperation on productivity and innovation. Through the Development Academy of the Philippines (DAP), designated as the country’s National Productivity Organization (NPO), the government implements and participates in APO programs designed to strengthen productivity, innovation capacity, and public-sector performance.

As NPO, the DAP hosts and coordinates a wide range of APO activities in the country, including international conferences, workshops, training programs, research initiatives, study missions, bilateral cooperation meetings, and e-learning projects. These initiatives promote public-sector productivity, good governance, and national competitiveness by providing Filipino institutions and professionals access to global expertise, tools, and best practices in productivity and innovation.

Support to the Productivity and Development Center (PDC) enables the Philippines to carry out administrative, technical, and liaison functions with the APO Secretariat in Tokyo and with counterpart NPOs across the 21 APO member economies. This ensures the country’s effective participation in APO programs and strengthens its role in the regional productivity movement.

column5: Department of the Interior and Local Government
column6:
The MEALGU Tier 1 funding is critical for enhancing governance and local development in the Philippines. It will primarily support the monitoring of projects under the 2025 Local Government Support Fund (LGSF), ensuring accountability, efficiency, and effective implementation. It also extends oversight to 2024 LGSF-funded initiatives, including programs like FALGU, SBDP, GEF, SAFP, and G3P, which foster community growth, sustainability, and equity.

A key focus is building the capacities of Local Government Units (LGUs) to manage infrastructure projects following the devolution of national functions. This investment empowers LGUs to address evolving local needs, fostering resilience and sustainable progress. The fund also supports monitoring Quick Impact Projects, a collaboration between India and the Philippines, designed to deliver immediate community benefits.

MEALGU Tier 2 builds on this by preparing LGUs for future challenges and opportunities, promoting resilience and innovation through targeted funding. It emphasizes transparency through Third-Party Monitoring and rigorous evaluation of all LGU infrastructure projects, ensuring alignment with national and global goals like the Philippine Development Plan and SDGs. Additionally, it reinforces the Build Better More Program, ensuring continued support for infrastructure development. Collectively, these efforts strengthen LGUs, drive accountability, and advance sustainable, community-focused progress.

column4: National Government Portal Project
column5: Department of Information and Communications Technology
column6:
The NGP Project is an initiative that aims to develop online portals and websites where government information, data, and services can be accessed. It also seeks to assist government units and sectoral groups in building robust digital platforms as part of enabling a whole-of-government digital transformation. The NGP supports the DICT in performing its mandate to establish a Filipino nation powered by ICT. It supports in providing universal access to quality, reliable, and secure ICT services, and contributes in boosting government efficiency, transparency and good governance through its systems development efforts.

The NGP implements the following components: 

Scoping and Development of Portals. The NGP will continuously oversee the operations, maintenance and enhancement of the existing NGP Portals:
Open Data Philippines (ODPh) Portal. The ODPh Portal is where government open data can be viewed and downloaded. 
GOVPH. The GOVPH is a web-based single window for all government information and services.
eBusiness/Central Business Portal (formerly PBH). The eBusiness/CBP, formerly known as the Philippine Business Hub (PBH), is an online portal where transactions related to business registration and/or renewal are coursed. For 2026, the eBusiness/CBP shall be enhanced to further improve ease of doing business in the country. 
Philippine Business Databank. The Philippine Business Databank (PBD) shall serve as a repository of data for all registered business entities. The system shall allow NGAs and LGUs to verify the validity, existence of, and other relevant information pertaining to business entities. The development of the system is in accordance with Section 14 of the Republic Act (RA) no. 11032 or the Ease of Doing Business Act of 2018.
eGovWeb. The eGovWeb is a content management system (CMS) that is designed to hasten the systems development of priority ICT programs. For 2026, the eGovWeb shall be implemented across other agencies, wherein it shall be for the use of government entities to harmonize the various government websites and ensure a level of quality among all government web content.
eGovDocs. The eGovDocs is a platform that is designed to streamline document handling for the Philippine government and citizens. It improves efficiency, security, and workflows while reducing paper use. For 2026, the eGovDocs will be set for further enhancement and implementation.

The Project also assists in the development of the e-Procurement System - Bidding Documents Module, a digital platform which aims to streamline the posting, processing and payments for procurement projects under DICT. For 2026, the NGP will also support the development of the Information Systems Strategic Planning (ISSP) Portal and Automation System to streamline and automate the preparation, submission, review, and approval of ISSPs.

Policy Implementation and Technical Support to Digitalization Initiatives. The NGP shall strengthen the foundations of its systems through effective policy-making on system usage. Furthermore, the Project team will also support the digitalization initiatives of other agencies through provision of technical assistance and support. The NGP team currently provides assistance to internal and inter-agency ICT initiatives such as the development of the eProcurement System - Bidding Documents module, Electronic Government Land Inventory System (eGLIS), and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) 2026 Website.

Project Management and Operations. This component shall provide support to the project implementation, particularly in its administrative and human resource requirements and activities. In addition, the team shall closely work with the Project Director, Bureau Directors, and the project leads in planning targets and activities, and in monitoring status and accomplishments of all initiatives.

Among the beneficiaries of the Project include national government agencies, local government units, business owners, and the general public.

column4: APPRENTICESHIP PROGRAM FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT OPERATIONS OFFICERS II AND III
column6:
Being the frontline of the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) to all Local Government Units (LGUs) in the country, the Local Government Operations Officers (LGOOs) represent the DILG in carrying out its mandates of general supervision and capacity building among LGUs. To equip these LGOOs with the necessary knowledge, skills, and attitudes to effectively represent the Department, a competency-building and developing program is prepared for them to undertake their current roles and duties and for them to take higher-level responsibilities in the future. Hence, the Apprenticeship Program for LGOOs II and III.

The Apprenticeship Program for LGOOs II and III is a flagship initiative of the Local Government Academy that was designed and institutionalized within the Department to cultivate future LGOOs in the field of local governance. This annual program is open to LGOO II & III position holders. It prepares them to take on the next higher position in the LGOO rank, engaging local governments toward excellence in local governance. The Records of Barangay Inhabitants (RBI) is a form of database being maintained and updated by the Barangay Secretary as mandated pursuant to Section 394(d)(6) of the Local Government Code of 1991 or RA 7160. Several enabling policies were issued by the DILG enjoining all local officials and Punong Barangays to ensure that all the barangays within their jurisdictions have completed or updated their RBIs. column4: Strengthening Local Governance (STRONGER) for Full Devolution
column5: Department of the Interior and Local Government
column6:
In line with the full devolution initiative of the national government pursuant to the implementation of the Supreme Court Ruling on the Mandanas and Garcia petitions, the Department provides continuous capacity-building initiatives to LGUs and coordinates with the members of the Committee on Devolution to operationalize the functions and services to be devolved to the LGUs and to be performed by the national government agencies. LGUs are expected to implement basic functions and services consistent with their respective capacities and priorities. This entails capacitating LGUs, through DILG Regional and Field Offices, and in monitoring the implementation of the devolved functions. 

Moreover, with the enactment of EO No. 14, s. 2023, LGUs are directed to adopt and undertake efforts to implement the PDP 2023-2028. To sustain initiatives on PDP localization and with the mainstreaming of the devolved functions in the local development plans, the DILG is proposing to facilitate the monitoring of the LGUs’ progress in terms of the alignment of local development plans with the attainment of PDP goals.

In addition to these, the DILG is also working closely with ULAP on the review of the LGC and update previously proposed amendments to Congress cognizant of the current developments in the local governance landscape and inherent inefficiencies that encourage fragmentation and perpetuate fiscal imbalances among LGUs.

Lastly, in line with EO No. 51, s. 2023, the Department, has been assigned the pivotal role of spearheading the expansion of Gender and Development (GAD) into Gender Equality, Disability, and Social Inclusion (GEDSI). GEDSI represents a comprehensive advocacy campaign aimed at addressing persistent challenges and barriers hindering the realization of full potential for women, people with disabilities, indigenous groups, LGBTQIA+ and other vulnerable sectors. In response, the DILG developed a comprehensive development intervention entitled the “Local Initiative in Governance and Social Protection (LINGAP) Program”. LINGAP intends to transform the Department into a gender-sensitive and inclusive organization, and to promote socially-protective organizations among local governments. This also paves the way for localizing and institutionalizing diversity and inclusion in the development of LGUs' CDP.

column4: Support to Upscaling Organizational Grit of Local Government Units (SULONG LGU)
column6:
As the primary institution that bridges the gap between the national government and local government units, the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) has been mandated to support the development of local governments. Section 9 of Executive Order No. 138 provides that the DILG, through its mandated training arm, the Local Government Academy (LGA), shall oversee the provision of capacity development interventions for local governments and develop the appropriate mechanisms to ensure the efficient utilization of government resources on this effort. Further, LGA had been tasked to harmonize all capacity development interventions by the DBM, NEDA, DOF, other NGAs, DAP, and third-party service providers for the LGUs. It is also tasked to optimize the potential of the Local Governance National and Regional Resource Centers as the convergence platform for capacity development.

A 2024 study on the state of devolution conducted by the Philippine Institute for Development Studies (PIDS) through an analysis of DTPs revealed a (i) high variation in LGU prioritization of devolved functions and LGU capacity, (ii) complete full devolution by 2024 is not achievable according to LGUs’ self-assessment, and (iii) capacity development interventions to aid the devolution agenda primarily focused on workforce and training requirements. Considering the diversity of local governments (i.e. local economies, capacities, priorities, constraints, and many others), the study finds that it is important to adopt appropriate approaches to service delivery based on the unique needs of LGUs.

Following the deadline set for the transition to full devolution, LGA’s 2024 Analysis of LGU Segmentation determined that 736 LGUs or 43.35% have high capacity and high performance (Quadant 1: Evolve), 295 LGUs or 17.37% have low capacity and high performance (Quadrant 2: Enable), 534 LGUs or 31.45% have low capacity and low performance (Quadrant 3: Engage), and 133 LGUs or 7.83% have high capacity and low performance (Quadrant 4: Energize). This analysis is based on the 2023 Seal of Good Local Governance data, with each quadrant representing a distinct grouping of LGUs with specific characteristics based on their compliance with capacity and performance indicators. 

The abovementioned data further reifies the diversity and uniqueness of local governments. For the Philippines, diversity is immediately apparent in geography and levels of urbanization and directly affects the state of local agriculture, environmental, and social welfare sectors. Even further, recognizing heterogeneity in context, performance, and capacity can help both the NG and LGUs better prepare and acquire the needed improvements to fulfill the goal of full devolution, and ultimately achieve the collective Ambisyon Natin 2040 of a matatag, maginhawa, at panatag na buhay for all Filipinos.

column4: Rising Leaders Development Program (RLDP)
column6:
The Rising Leaders’ Development Program (RLDP) is a nationwide initiative of the Development Academy of the Philippines (DAP) that directly addresses the leadership development gap among young public servants and youth-serving professionals aged 18-30. While most capacity-building programs are geared toward mid- and senior-level officials, RLDP responds to the urgent need for structured, values-driven, and innovation-oriented training for junior officers, Sangguniang Kabataan officials, student leaders, and emerging youth professionals in government, civil society, and local communities.

RLDP follows a ladderized three-phase framework that balances inclusivity with depth of learning. In the Open-Learning Track, more than 2,000 youth leaders nationwide will participate in four hybrid modules on youth governance, leadership, nationalism, and innovation. Completers will receive DAP-issued certificates. From this pool, 100 fellows will advance to the Fellowship Track- a one-month intensive program combining advanced learning, mentorship, and the design of Change Initiative Projects. The journey culminates in the Follow-Through Phase, a three-month period of mentoring and peer collaboration to help fellows refine and implement their initiatives within their institutions and communities. A special feature is the international immersion, where the top 10 fellows will join a one-week program with partner institutions abroad- exposing them to global leadership and governance models while inspiring community-rooted reforms upon their return.

Grounded in RLDP’s Five Domains- Nationalism and Foundational Leadership, Ethical Leadership and Public Service Values, Practical Governance Processes, Systems Thinking and Behavioral Insights, and Innovation and Digital Transformation- he program builds a principled and future-ready leadership pipeline. By combining broad participation with immersive fellowship experiences, RLDP ensures that young Filipino leaders are not only trained, but truly empowered to lead reforms, foster accountability, and drive innovation in Philippine governance today.

column4: National Productivity Development Agenda (NPDA)
column6:
The National Productivity Development Agenda (NPDA) 2026–2028 is a comprehensive framework that institutionalizes productivity as a driver of inclusive and sustainable growth. It supports national development priorities under the Philippine Development Plan (PDP) 2023–2028, AmBisyon Natin 2040, and the Bagong Pilipinas agenda. The PDP 2023–2028 Midterm Update, Chapter 14 (Outcome 3: Government functions, systems, and mechanisms rationalized and strengthened), underscores the need to “raise the productivity performance of agencies” and provides that “for a more coherent national productivity strategy, the National Productivity Development Agenda will be developed.” In line with this mandate, the NPDA will harmonize productivity initiatives across public and private sectors, ensuring coherence, alignment, and measurable outcomes.

The NPDA adopts a phased approach. In 2026 (Formulation Phase), the program will develop the NPDA through multi-stakeholder consultations, establish baseline productivity data, and design a monitoring, measurement, and evaluation framework. In 2027–2028 (Advocacy and Implementation Phase), it will undertake nationwide advocacy, capacity-building programs, and phased roll-out of productivity strategies, with regular updating to align with the PDP cycle. Key components include: (1) NPDA Formulation and Productivity Measurement (baseline study, indicators, and M&E framework); (2) Capability Development and Technical Assistance (training, workshops, and APO-aligned productivity specialist development); and (3) Advocacy, Promotion, and Partnerships (nationwide campaigns, incentive mechanisms, and knowledge products), supported by sectoral and thematic stakeholder consultations at national and regional levels.

column4: Strengthening Philippine Quality Award Administration and Provision of Business Excellence Solutions for Transformation (BEST)
column6:
The Philippine Quality Award (PQA) was established in 1997 through Republic Act 9013 as the country’s highest level of recognition for organizational performance excellence. From its inception, the Development Academy of the Philippines (DAP) has been one of the intellectual and technical brains behind the PQA, helping craft its framework and adapting international standards to the Philippine context. 

Today, DAP continues to play a pivotal role as the Vice Chair of the PQA Executive Committee and as the designated Award Administrator for the public sector. In these capacities, DAP ensures that the PQA remains a credible, rigorous, and transformative program that guides both private and government organizations in their pursuit of quality, productivity, and good governance.

As the PQA Award Administrator, DAP is responsible for the full cycle of implementation, from promoting the award or inviting public sector organizations to join, to managing applications, and assisting the assessors during the conduct of assessments. The DAP also builds institutional capability by training agencies on self-assessment, developing sector-specific tools, and disseminating best practices. These interventions have positioned the PQA not only as a recognition mechanism but as a national driver for continuous improvement, performance excellence, and competitiveness across the public sector.

To sustain and expand these initiatives, adequate government funding through the General Appropriations Act (GAA) is critical. The PQA is a national undertaking that directly contributes to improved governance and service delivery, yet it requires significant investments in sustaining and developing the assessors including the different capability-building programs needed to capacitate the assessors. Without sufficient resources, the program risks losing momentum and failing to reach more public sector agencies that stand to benefit most from its transformative framework. Funding the PQA under the GAA ensures continuity, credibility, and inclusiveness, allowing the government to institutionalize a culture of excellence that translates into more efficient, accountable, and citizen-centered services.

Equally important to sustaining the Philippine Quality Award Administration is the provision of government support for the Business Excellence Solutions for Transformation (BEST) Program. While the PQA sets the benchmark for performance excellence, the BEST Program operationalizes it by serving as a structured handholding scheme for organizations. Many public sector agencies and institutions are initially hesitant to apply for the PQA because they feel unprepared to meet its rigorous standards. The BEST Program addresses this gap by guiding them step by step, through self-assessment, capability-building, and technical guidance through workshops and coaching, so that they can gradually build the internal capability and confidence needed to adopt the PQA framework.

BEST Program ensures that the benefits of the PQA are not limited to a select few but cascaded widely across the bureaucracy, where it allows public sector agencies to systematically strengthen their processes, align with global standards of excellence, and foster a culture of continuous improvement even before they formally enter the award cycle. By supporting the BEST Program under the GAA, the government is in effect investing in a developmental pathway that not only prepares organizations for recognition but also equips them to consistently deliver the highest quality services to citizens.

column4: Local Institutional and Fiscal Transformation (LIFT) Program
column6:
LIFT introduces a structured, multi-year capacity development program designed to equip LGUs with the governance foundations, sectoral capabilities, and institutional mechanisms necessary to deliver high-quality, standards-aligned services in a fully devolved environment. It will be delivered through a structured combination of training, technical assistance, organizational development, sectoral capability building, and institutionalization support to ensure LGU readiness for full devolution.

By enhancing competencies, clarifying roles, improving governance systems, and embedding performance and accountability mechanisms into regular operations, the program supports LGUs in converting fiscal capacity into measurable service delivery outcomes, with the following pillars:

Pillar 1: Leadership and Governance Competency Strengthening - Strengthens LGU leadership, strategic management capability, and decision-making readiness across all phases of the devolution transition.
Pillar 2: Insitutional and Systems Development - Builds and embeds organizational systems, processes, and performance mechanisms that enable consistent, standards-aligned service delivery.
PIllar 3: Sectoral, Technology and Digital Transformation - Enhances sector-specific competencies and accelerates digital and technological integration to improve service quality, efficiency, and innovation.

The LIFT Program will be implemented over a six-year period, using a phased and modular approach aligned with LGU readiness and regional diversity,

Phase 1 (Year 1-2): Pilot and Learning Design- Pilot testing (10% of LGU) of courses and technical assistance, baseline assessment, refinement of approaches 
Phase 2 (Year 2-3): Foundational Capability Building - Establish core governance foundation and readiness for transformation 
Phase 3 (Year 3-4): Sectoral Deepening and Systems Development - Strengthen sector-specific capacities and systems development aligned with service delivery standards.
Phase 4 (Year 4-5) Scaling up and institutionalization - Scaling up of training (credit-bearing professionalization) and technical assistance, and institutionalizing of tools and adaptive systems.
Phase 5 (Year 5-6): National roll-out and Sustainability - Mainstreaming and integration to DAP and DILG-LGA Programs.

Through blended learning, on-site coaching, peer learning clusters, and sustained technical assistance, the program ensures reforms are embedded, operational, and scalable nationwide.

column4: Digital Government Program
column5: Department of Information and Communications Technology
column6:
The program seeks to expand the deployment, implementation, and operations of its priority eGovernment platforms through a whole-of-government approach, addressing fragmentation, interoperability issues, and improving citizen experience through integrated digital systems. The program supports the continued national and provincial rollout of the following platforms:

Electronic Local Government Unit (eLGU) System - Streamlines local
government services by integrating key modules such as the Business Permit and Licensing System (BPLS), Local Civil Registry, eCedula, Working and Building Permit Systems, Barangay Clearance, Citizen Information Dissemination, and LGU Centralized News. It aims to reduce bureaucratic bottlenecks and enhance service efficiency in cities and municipalities. As part of the strategy, the DICT, in coordination with DILG, DTI, and ARTA, has conducted nationwide eLGU Caravans to promote adoption and provide technical support to LGUs.
Digital National ID - The DICT and PSA successfully launched the first Digital National ID where citizens can now use their mobile phones, with or without internet, as their identification card. This will simplify submission of documents, data gathering and integration of multiple national and local government services, including private-relying parties in a single identification system. The Digital National ID can be accessed via the eGovPH app, another first in the Philippine government allowing citizens to access government services in a single platform. This will simplify the way people interact with the
government even at the comfort of their homes. This official digital version of the National ID serves as valid proof of identification and streamlines transactions across government and private institutions.
Travel Information System (eTravel) - Consolidates multiple arrival and
departure-related processes (e.g., health declarations, customs forms, OEC, etc.) into a single platform for international travelers. The system supports paperless, seamless travel and is currently deployed in 18 international airports and 35 seaports. SMS Messaging System (eMessage) - Enables secure and wide-scale delivery of SMS-based notifications to support user authentication, two-factor verification, and public information dissemination for eGovernment services, while remaining compliant with the Data Privacy Act of 2012.

Direct Beneficiaries
1. Government Agencies and Local Government Units (LGUs)
a. eLGU System: A total of 952 LGUs implementing the Business
Permit and Licensing System, 467 with Barangay Business
Clearance, 160 with Building Permit Systems, 106 with Working
Permit Systems, and 113 with eCedula and Local Civil Registry
are direct beneficiaries. These digitized systems streamline LGU
operations, reduce manual processes, and enhance the quality
and speed of service delivery at the local level.

2. Filipino Citizens
a. eTravel Users: Over 46 million passengers have benefited from
the eTravel system, which offers a seamless, paperless, and faster
travel process, especially at ports of entry and exit, enhancing
convenience and reducing processing time.
b. eMessage Users: Citizens directly benefit from eMessage, which
facilitates real-time communication and official notifications from
government agencies, ensuring timely updates, improved
transparency, and greater trust in public services.

Indirect Beneficiaries
1. Other Government Agencies and the Private Sector
a. The eLGU system’s integration with national platforms reduces
manual processes, improves data accuracy, and speeds up
coordination across departments.
b. eTravel streamlines coordination between various agencies,
allowing them to operate more efficiently and allocate resources
better.
c. eMessage enhances inter-agency communication and public
outreach, indirectly benefitting agencies and private entities
relying on timely information dissemination.

2. General Public and Communities
a. Through the improved efficiency and responsiveness of LGUs
via eLGU, communities experience faster processing of permits,
reduced bureaucratic delays, and improved local governance.
b. eTravel indirectly supports the economy by facilitating smoother
movement of people, encouraging tourism, and improving the
travel experience.
c. eMessage helps ensure that critical government information
reaches broader audiences quickly, especially in times of
emergencies, public health updates, or disaster response.
Overall, the DigiGov Program seeks to significantly enhance service delivery, accessibility, and operational efficiency across government sectors. Focusing on key initiatives such as eLGU, eTravel, and eMessage, the program directly benefits government units and Filipino citizens while also creating indirect value for broader stakeholders through improved digital infrastructure and processes.

column4: Mainstreaming Futures Thinking and Emerging Technologies in Government - Capacity Development Trainings and Conference
column6:
In pursuit of DAP’s mandate to capacitate individuals and development stakeholder organizations in government, the GSPDM has set its sights to take in stride the national goals on developing and protecting the capabilities of individuals and families and on fostering an enabling environment for social and economic transformation. These goals are embodied in the substantive Chapters 2-15 of the Philippine Development Plan 2023-2028, framed by the 8-Point Socioeconomic Agenda of President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. and the AmBisyon Natin 2040. In the same manner, the GSPDM also considers the achievement of the global and national agenda of achieving the 17 Sustainable Development Goals.

Governments today operate in an increasingly complex and rapidly changing environment. Emerging technologies, shifting socio-economic dynamics, and global trends require public servants to anticipate change, make informed decisions, and design policies that are resilient and future-ready.

Foresight and futures thinking provide frameworks and methodologies that enable governments to systematically explore plausible futures, identify opportunities and risks, and integrate forward-looking perspectives into policy-making. Despite their potential, these approaches remain underutilized in many government agencies.

The GSPDM is proud to introduce the Futures Studies Platform, an integrated ideation hub designed to cultivate futures literacy, anticipatory leadership, and long-range strategic thinking across government, academia, industry, and civil society. Serving as a nexus for innovation, dialogue, and collaborative imagination, the platform envisions a future-ready Philippines where leaders and institutions can navigate uncertainty, harness emerging opportunities, and co-create preferred futures for the nation. This program seeks to mainstream foresight, futures thinking, and emerging technology awareness across government agencies. It also aims to transform public sector leaders into strategic foresight practitioners capable of anticipating trends, designing innovative policies, and leveraging technology to create resilient governance systems that address both present and future societal needs.

From 2020-2023, the GSPDM conducted six (6) batches of the CCFFT, the latest one of which is a scholarship program, benefiting 40 students. In 2024, three CCFFT batches, with forty (40) students each, will be implemented for 120 scholarship beneficiaries, to be underwritten by the prior year’s residual and current year’s funding of the program. The GSPDM hopes to continue its implementation in the succeeding years by offering a scholarship program for public sector employees. Consistent with the program design, the scholars will be required to submit, present, and implement a Policy Brief, which is the major final output of the program. The CCFFT will engage local and international FT experts as faculty of the class and in its Hiraya Talks, an interactive virtual segment that features world futurists and experts who would share various futures perspectives and innovations.  

Taking off from the gains of the CCFFT, the GSPDM has developed the curriculum for the MPM, Major in Futures Studies, the first ever master’s program in the Philippines that focuses on the professional practice of FT. Recently approved by the Academic Council, the GSPDM hopes to offer this program through a scholarship grant to employees in the public sector.

At the center of the platform is Philippine Shared Futures 2050, a national visioning and scenario-building initiative that aims to co-create long-term development pathways for the country. Through multi-sector engagements, collaborative foresight workshops, and strategic dialogues, this initiative will serve as both a strategic roadmap and a catalyst for future-informed governance and societal transformation. 

To broaden public engagement, GSPDM will also launch the Futures Dash Talk Series, a dynamic and accessible platform featuring concise, high-impact presentations on key foresight concepts and emerging trends. The series will showcase the policy foresight papers produced by CCFFT batches, providing a venue for learners to present their insights, preferred futures, and strategic recommendations.

As an integrated ideation hub, the Futures Studies Platform brings together education, research, public engagement, and national visioning, strengthening GSPDM’s commitment to embedding futures thinking at the heart of governance and development. Through this platform, GSPDM aims to ensure that the Philippines does not merely adapt to the future but actively shapes it.

By facilitating capacity development workshops and high-level conferences, the initiative fosters not only individual skill development but also institutional culture change—embedding a mindset of innovation, strategic anticipation, and future-readiness within the public sector. Ultimately, this program contributes to a government that is not only responsive but also visionary, adaptive, and transformative, ready to meet the challenges and opportunities of the 21st century.

column4: Modernization of Local Government Academy Training Center in Los Baños, Laguna
column6:
For more than five decades, the Local Government Academy Training Center (LGATC) has stood as one of the country’s most enduring institutions for shaping community development workers and newly elected local officials—especially during each election cycle when leadership transitions demand immediate, high-quality training. Situated within the University of the Philippines Los Baños campus, the LGATC has played a vital role in transforming leadership mindsets, strengthening public service values, and elevating the competencies of local governments nationwide.

However, after years of limited investment and exposure to environmental stressors, the Training Center has reached a critical state of disrepair. In the past decade, utilization dropped sharply due to structural deterioration—primarily within the dormitory complex and the main building’s wooden framework. The facility’s 80% timber construction has rotted extensively, with beams, posts, and floorboards suffering irreversible termite damage. DPWH’s engineering inspections confirmed that the dormitory and major portions of the main building can no longer be safely repaired. Failures in roofing, ceiling collapse, structural gaps, and weakened beams—further aggravated by Typhoon Kristine in 2024—have rendered the building unsafe for occupancy.

Because of this, the LGA is now forced to conduct capacity-building activities in hotels and private venues—an arrangement that costs significantly more and restricts the number of participants we can serve, directly limiting LGA’s mandate to strengthen LGUs.

Need for Demolition and Full Replacement of the Dormitory
The dormitory is central to LGA’s training model, as most programs require immersive, live-in capacity development. DPWH’s updated 2025 engineering assessment recommends complete demolition and reconstruction due to:
•        Total degradation of wooden structural components
•        Weakened load-bearing capacity
•        Damage from falling pine trees during Typhoon Kristine
•        Ceiling collapse and water infiltration
•        Persistent safety hazards from termite infestation

The facility is beyond economical repair. Rebuilding is the only safe and cost-efficient solution to restore LGATC to full functionality.

Urgent Rehabilitation of Magsaysay Hall
Magsaysay Hall—historically the main venue for lectures, plenaries, and LGU leadership programs—also requires urgent upgrading. The hall suffers chronic water leakage due to its internal gutter roofing design, which traps water during heavy rainfall. This has led to recurring damage to ceilings, walls, and interior finishes, compromising both safety and acoustics. DPWH’s 2025 estimate includes complete replacement of the roof and damaged wall sections to prevent further deterioration.

Importance of the Covered Court for Health and Well-Being
The covered court is essential not only as a multipurpose activity area but also for supporting the physical and mental wellbeing of trainees—many of whom undergo intensive, multi-week leadership programs. Providing a safe, weather-protected space for exercise, group dynamics, and stress-relieving activities is critical in maintaining the well-being and productivity of participants. DPWH’s updated estimate for the construction of the covered court ensures that the training environment remains holistic, resilient, and conducive to learning.
 
Updated Funding Requirements Based on DPWH 2025 Estimates
Reflecting the latest DPWH engineering validation and cost estimates (2025), the following are required: 

The total floor area of the Main Building or Dormitory is 1,687.30 sqm

These updated estimates reflect DPWH’s technical assessment of what is necessary to restore LGATC as a safe, modern, and resilient national training institution.

column4: MIMAROPA Local Governance Strengthening Project
column5: Department of the Interior and Local Government
column6: The project focuses on strengthening the capacity of Local Government Units (LGUs) in the MIMAROPA region, a core mandate of the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG). Effective capacity development enables LGUs to deliver responsive services and implement relevant Programs, Projects, and Activities (PPAs) that meet the needs of their constituents and support developmental goals. However, several challenges hinder this process: LGUs are not utilizing existing capacity assessment tools; interventions from stakeholders such as DILG, national government agencies (NGAs), non-government organizations (NGOs), and other offices are often misaligned with actual LGU needs; and there is no proper Monitoring and Evaluation (M&E) system to assess the effectiveness of these programs. As a result, interventions tend to be short-term and lack strategic impact. To address these issues, the project emphasizes the proper formulation and evaluation of the LGU Capacity Development Agenda (CDA), ensuring that capacity development providers are informed of the results and can respond to identified gaps. The initiative targets all 78 Provincial, City, and Municipal LGUs (PCMs) in the MIMAROPA region.
